title: The Silent Port Drought
subtitle: Unpooled outbound HTTP connections trap 28,000 sockets in TIME_WAIT, causing total outage

brief.narrative: A code-red Amber Alert is triggered for an abducted 6-year-old child in a stolen minivan. The department's Emergency Dispatch Alert Service begins blasting outbound SMS and cellular push notifications to 200,000 registered neighborhood watch members at 3,000 HTTP requests/second via an external regional telecommunications gateway (`api.telecom.state.gov:443`). For the first 10 seconds, everything works smoothly. Then, at second 15, the entire notification system catastrophically collapses. Every subsequent outbound call fails instantly with OS socket error `connect: cannot assign requested address (EADDRNOTAVAIL)`. The dispatch application code was creating a brand new HTTP client instance with `Connection: close` for every single outbound message. In TCP, the combination of (Source IP, Source Port, Destination IP, Destination Port) uniquely identifies a socket. With a single destination gateway, the operating system kernel allocated all ~28,232 ephemeral ports (range 32768 to 60999). As requests closed, sockets were trapped in the mandatory 60-second `TIME_WAIT` state, exhausting all available ports and paralyzing the emergency broadcast.
symptoms: Outbound emergency alert dispatch crashed abruptly 15 seconds into high-throughput broadcast
Application logs flooded with `EADDRNOTAVAIL: Cannot assign requested address` errors
Host operating system socket metric `netstat -an | grep TIME_WAIT | wc -l` hit 28,232
Outgoing network bandwidth and CPU are practically idle (< 5%) during the outage
brief.objective: Diagnose ephemeral port exhaustion caused by unpooled short-lived TCP sockets in TIME_WAIT and configure HTTP Keep-Alive connection pooling with kernel socket reuse.

rootCause.question: What is the root cause of the sudden `EADDRNOTAVAIL` socket error halting the Amber Alert broadcast?

options.text: Ephemeral port exhaustion caused by high-frequency short-lived HTTP connections without Keep-Alive: creating a new TCP socket per request filled all ~28,000 available OS source ports, trapping them in the 60-second TIME_WAIT state
options.feedback: Correct! A TCP connection is uniquely identified by the 4-tuple: (Source IP, Source Port, Destination IP, Destination Port). When an application calls a single upstream IP:Port (the Telecom Gateway) without connection reuse (`Connection: close`), each outbound request consumes a temporary local source port (ephemeral port) from the kernel's range (32768–60999, ~28,000 ports). When closed, TCP sockets are required by RFC 793 to linger in `TIME_WAIT` for 2*MSL (60 seconds) to ensure stray packets dissipate. At 3,000 req/sec, all 28,000 ports depleted in under 10 seconds, causing subsequent `connect()` calls to fail immediately with `EADDRNOTAVAIL`.

options.text: The State Telecom Gateway's firewall detected a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack and blacklisted the police IP address
options.feedback: The gateway logs confirm it never blocked the client; inbound traffic simply stopped arriving. Furthermore, `EADDRNOTAVAIL` is a client-side operating system error indicating no local port could be assigned before any packet ever left the machine.

options.text: The alert service exhausted its open file descriptor (FD) limit due to unclosed file handles on the local disk
options.feedback: If file descriptors were exhausted, the OS would return `EMFILE: Too many open files`. The error was explicitly `EADDRNOTAVAIL: Cannot assign requested address`, indicating ephemeral port exhaustion in the IP stack.

options.text: The telecom gateway's SSL certificate expired, causing TLS handshakes to abort immediately
options.feedback: TLS certificate errors produce `CERT_HAS_EXPIRED` or handshake failure codes during the TLS negotiation, not socket allocation failures during initial TCP binding.

fix.question: How should the dispatch service and host OS be configured to support high-throughput outbound notifications without exhausting ports?

options.text: Enable HTTP Keep-Alive with persistent connection pooling in the HTTP client to reuse established TCP sockets across requests, upgrade to HTTP/2 multiplexing, and enable `tcp_tw_reuse` in the kernel
options.feedback: Correct! Enabling HTTP Keep-Alive with a connection pool (e.g., maintaining a pool of 200–500 persistent TCP connections) allows hundreds of thousands of HTTP requests to pipeline across existing sockets without constantly creating and destroying TCP connections. Upgrading to HTTP/2 allows multiplexing multiple concurrent streams over a handful of sockets. Finally, setting `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse = 1` safely allows outgoing connections to reuse sockets in `TIME_WAIT` when timestamp matching is valid.

options.text: Rewrite the notification service to use raw UDP datagrams without error checking or delivery confirmations
options.feedback: The external Telecom Gateway exposes an HTTPS REST API. Unilaterally sending UDP packets to an HTTPS port will fail completely, as the remote server expects a valid TLS over TCP handshake.

options.text: Reduce outbound throughput to 50 requests per second so that sockets naturally clear TIME_WAIT before ports run out
options.feedback: Limiting throughput to 50 req/s means dispatching an Amber Alert to 200,000 citizens would take over an hour, fatally compromising child recovery efforts.

options.text: Reboot the operating system host machine every 15 seconds to flush the kernel's network socket tables
options.feedback: Rebooting the server every 15 seconds results in massive downtime, continuous service disruption, and fails to solve the architectural flaw of unpooled connections.
